header: Three ways an otherwise-correct answer can quietly mislead. I read them from the model's SQL; I do not ask a model:

1. LIMIT over GROUPS ("which department has the most ..." as ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 1). If two departments tie for first, one silently disappears. Ranking with rank() keeps every row tied for the place.
2. A grouped result with no ORDER BY: the rows come back in an arbitrary order.
3. A list of PEOPLE not in seniority order (global_seniority_rank): people in the same grade come back in whatever order the database happens to use.

4. A window function in the OUTER query next to a filter on a window result from the sub-query (rank() ... WHERE r = 1 together with sum(cnt) OVER () ). The outer window runs AFTER the filter, so the "total" is only the winners' own count and a percentage of the total comes out as 100.
5. A list of names inside one cell (array_agg / string_agg) with no ORDER BY: the names come in arbitrary order.

6. Ranking BEFORE the population is decided: the outer WHERE holds both the rank cut (r <= 10) and another condition (nonexec_count = 0). The rank was computed over ALL rows, so the top 10 of everyone is cut first and then thinned: fewer than 10 rows come back. The condition that decides who competes belongs in HAVING/WHERE of the ranking query.
I made the pipeline give the model ONE chance to fix it (first attempt only); it never fails a question over this.

symbols.name: COMPARISON_CUE
doc: "Who is more senior, A or B?" answered with ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 shows ONE person: nobody can see whether the other was found, or either rank. I require the answer to show BOTH people with their global_seniority_rank (lower = more senior). I judge this only when the QUESTION is an explicit comparison ("more/less senior", "who is senior/junior", "senior/junior between/among", "which of ... senior"), so "the most senior Roy or Ray" (a genuine LIMIT 1) is left alone.

symbols.name: JUNIOR_CUE
doc: This is the sentence that STATES the answer of a comparison, in plain words. Code computes it from the data, never the model. global_seniority_rank = grade level x 10,000 + position within that grade (lower = more senior). The number itself means nothing to a reader, so I make the sentence speak of grades and of position in the grade's seniority list instead. Domain rule: among EXECUTIVES the order within a grade is real (earlier in HR's list = more senior). Among NON-EXECUTIVES only the grade order is meaningful, so I never rank two non-executives of one grade against each other.
